371.event_title: Ino Tadataka begins his survey of Japan at fifty-five
371.place: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, Japan
371.event: In 1800, at the age of 55, Ino Tadataka obtained the shogunate's permission to survey the southeastern coast of Hokkaido, partly in order to work out the length of a degree of latitude. His maps impressed the shogunate, which sent him on survey after survey along the coasts of Japan over the next sixteen years, during which he spent more than 3,700 days on the road and covered tens of thousands of kilometres on foot. He died in 1818, and the completed map of Japan based on his surveys was presented to the shogunate in 1821.
371.explanation: Ino began the work for which he is remembered at an age when most men of his time had retired, and his tireless persistence produced the first accurate map of Japan.
371.tie_back: The kural says that when fortune is set on bringing gain it shows itself as unflagging effort, and Ino's late-life energy, which carried him around the whole country, is the kind of perseverance the couplet describes.
371._accuracy_note: A vivid example of tireless effort leading to success, but whether that effort was itself a sign of fate, as the kural claims, cannot be shown historically, and the sloth half of the kural is not illustrated.

372.place: Moscow and the road from Moscow to the Niemen River, Russian Empire
372.event: In June 1812 Napoleon, then the most successful general in Europe, invaded Russia with a force usually estimated at between 450,000 and 600,000 men. The Russian armies retreated, and after the costly Battle of Borodino in September he entered a largely deserted Moscow, much of which was soon destroyed by fire. He waited there about five weeks for Tsar Alexander I to offer peace, which never came, and left on 19 October; by the end of the winter retreat only a small fraction of his army remained.
372.explanation: The campaign is a classic example of a commander with an unmatched record of victories making a series of misjudgements that destroyed his army and began the end of his empire.
372.tie_back: The kural says a fate of loss makes even the clever act foolishly, and Napoleon's long, fruitless wait in Moscow as winter approached is often cited as the moment his famous judgement failed him.
372._accuracy_note: A well-known case of a brilliant leader's judgement failing as fortune turned, though historians explain it by strategy and circumstance rather than fate, and the troop figures are estimates.

373.event_title: Ramanujan writes to G. H. Hardy
373.place: Madras (Chennai), India, and Trinity College, Cambridge, England
373.event: Srinivasa Ramanujan, who had no university degree, taught himself higher mathematics largely from G. S. Carr's Synopsis, a dated book that listed thousands of results with only the briefest proofs, and then went far beyond it with his own discoveries. On 16 January 1913, while working as a clerk in Madras, he wrote to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, enclosing around 120 theorems. Hardy, though puzzled by the absence of conventional proofs, recognised his genius and arranged for him to come to Cambridge, where Ramanujan was later elected a Fellow of Trinity College.
373.explanation: Ramanujan's mathematics came from a powerful insight of his own that no textbook had given him, and it astonished scholars trained in far more learning.
373.tie_back: The kural says that however many subtle books a person studies, it is the understanding that is truly their own that prevails, and Ramanujan's original genius, nourished by a single old book, outran what formal learning could teach.
373._accuracy_note: A strong example of innate understanding outweighing book learning, though the kural's claim that this understanding is allotted by fate goes beyond what history can show.

374.event_title: Spinoza declines the chair of philosophy at Heidelberg
374.place: The Hague, Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands)
374.event: Baruch (Benedict de) Spinoza, expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656, supported himself by grinding optical lenses and lived in modest rented rooms. In 1673 he was offered the chair of philosophy at the University of Heidelberg but declined it, out of concern that he would not have complete freedom to teach as he wished. He died in 1677, and his Ethics, published after his death, became one of the most influential works of Western philosophy.
374.explanation: One of the great minds of the seventeenth century lived and died with very little money, while his ideas proved far more valuable than any fortune.
374.tie_back: The kural says fate works in two different ways, so that becoming wealthy is one thing and becoming wise is another, and Spinoza's life of modest lens-grinding alongside his towering philosophy shows how separate the two can be.
374._accuracy_note: Spinoza illustrates the gap between wisdom and wealth well, though his modest means were partly his own choice rather than purely the work of fortune.

375.event_title: William Perkin's failed quinine experiment produces mauve
375.event: In 1856 the eighteen-year-old chemistry student William Henry Perkin was trying, in a home laboratory in London, to make quinine, the costly anti-malaria drug, from coal-tar chemicals. The experiment failed, but it left a dark residue from which he extracted a brilliant purple substance that could dye silk. He patented it in August 1856 as mauve, the first synthetic dye, set up a factory with his father's help, and the success of his dyes made him rich enough to retire from business in his thirties.
375.explanation: Perkin's discovery turned coal tar, a waste product, into the raw material of a vast new chemical industry.
375.tie_back: The kural says that in the pursuit of wealth fortune can turn unfavourable circumstances into favourable ones, and Perkin's failed attempt at a medicine became the source of his fortune and of the synthetic dye industry.
375._accuracy_note: A clear documented reversal in which a failure became a source of wealth; only the opposite direction of the kural, good turning bad, is not shown.

376.event_title: Steve Jobs leaves Apple and returns
376.event: In 1985 Steve Jobs, who had co-founded Apple Computer in 1976, lost a boardroom power struggle with chief executive John Sculley, was removed from running the Macintosh division and left the company to found NeXT. In early 1997 Apple, which needed a new operating system, bought NeXT, and Jobs returned, becoming interim chief executive later that year. Under his leadership the struggling company recovered and went on to become one of the most valuable companies in the world.
376.explanation: Jobs lost the company he had founded, yet a decade later Apple came back to him through the very company he had started after being pushed out.
376.tie_back: The kural says that what is truly one's own will not leave even if it is carried off and thrown away, and Apple, lost by Jobs in 1985, returned to him in 1997.
376._accuracy_note: A famous case of something lost coming back, though Jobs's return was the result of business decisions and does not show the kural's other half, that what is not ours cannot be kept.

377.event_title: Alexander the Great dies at Babylon
377.event: By 323 BCE Alexander the Great had conquered the Persian Empire, taking possession of its royal treasuries, and ruled lands stretching from Greece to the Indus. In Babylon, while planning an expedition to Arabia and new projects for irrigation and sea routes, he fell ill after a banquet and died in June 323 BCE at the age of 32. He left no clear successor, and his generals soon fought one another and divided his empire.
377.explanation: The ruler who had gathered more wealth and territory than anyone before him had almost no time to enjoy any of it.
377.tie_back: The kural says that even those who amass vast wealth can enjoy it only to the extent fate allows, and Alexander, master of the treasures of Persia, died within a few years of winning them.
377._accuracy_note: A striking gap between possession and enjoyment, though the cause of his death remains uncertain and the kural speaks of ordinary wealth rather than conquest.

378.event_title: Carolina Maria de Jesus publishes her favela diary
378.event: Carolina Maria de Jesus, a Black single mother of three, lived in a shack in a Sao Paulo favela and supported her children by collecting paper and scrap to sell, writing a diary in notebooks she found in the rubbish. Her diary of the years 1955 to 1960 was published in Sao Paulo in 1960 as Quarto de Despejo, later translated into English as Child of the Dark. It described hunger and daily struggle in plain terms and became one of the best-selling books in Brazilian history.
378.explanation: Her diary showed readers that poverty is not a peaceful simplicity but a daily round of hunger, worry and hard labour.
378.tie_back: The kural observes that the destitute, who have nothing, would seem ready to renounce the world, yet fate still makes them taste the hardships allotted to them, and de Jesus's diary records how having little brought not detachment but constant struggle.
378._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the diary documents that poverty brings suffering rather than detachment, but this compressed kural about renunciation and allotted suffering has no close historical illustration.

379.event_title: Shackleton's men survive the loss of the Endurance
379.place: Weddell Sea, Elephant Island and South Georgia, Antarctica and the South Atlantic
379.event: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance, carrying his expedition to cross Antarctica, was trapped in the Weddell Sea ice in January 1915 and slowly crushed, and the crew abandoned her in October 1915. Shackleton gave up the original goal and turned the expedition into an effort to save every man: they camped on the ice for months, sailed in open boats to Elephant Island, and Shackleton and five others then crossed some 800 miles of ocean to South Georgia to fetch help. After several attempts he rescued the men left on Elephant Island in August 1916, and none of the Endurance crew died.
379.explanation: Shackleton accepted the collapse of his great ambition without despair and put all his energy into the new task that misfortune had handed him.
379.tie_back: The kural asks why those who welcome good fortune should be distressed by bad, since both come from the same fate, and Shackleton met the loss of his ship and his goal with the same steady purpose he had brought to the expedition's hopeful start.
379._accuracy_note: Shackleton's composure in disaster is well documented in outline, but the sources record his actions more than his inner equanimity, so the fit is partly inferred.

380.event_title: The royal family's flight to Varennes
380.event: On the night of 20-21 June 1791 King Louis XVI, Queen Marie Antoinette and their children left the Tuileries palace in Paris in disguise, hoping to reach loyal troops near the eastern frontier. At Sainte-Menehould the postmaster's son, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, recognised the travellers and took steps that led to the royal party being stopped and arrested when they reached Varennes. They were escorted back to Paris, arriving on 25 June, and the failed escape destroyed much of the public's remaining trust in the monarchy.
380.explanation: A carefully planned escape not only failed but hastened the very downfall it was meant to avoid.
380.tie_back: The kural asks what is mightier than fate, since even when a person devises another way out, fate arrives first, and at Varennes the king's planned escape was overtaken a short distance from safety.
380._accuracy_note: A vivid case of a planned escape being overtaken, though the failure is explained historically by delays and recognition rather than by fate.
